papers.title: Cold atmospheric plasma for improved sustainability and fish welfare in recirculating aquaculture systems
papers.abstract: Decontamination of water is mandatory for the cultivation of aquatic species in recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS). Avoiding economic and ecological losses while ensuring safe conditions is important for the future introduction of new technologies. Therefore, the implementation of cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) within RAS was examined for the first time. For the integration of this technology two equal RAS were set up, one using CAP, the other one ultraviolet light (UV) for water decontamination. Experiments with Rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) were performed for three weeks to compare CAP with UV as reference. The CAP device was switched on intermittently for 8 hours daily (with intervals of 10 min on and 30 min off), while two UV lamps were turned on continuously throughout the entire time of 3 weeks, which required more energy. Fish development was tracked by fish weight and stress levels (cortisol measurements). Values for pH, conductivity, oxygen, temperature, microbial load, microbiome and ion composition were also monitored. Microbial loads for both setups were reduced by four orders of magnitude. The biodiversity of the microbiome of the two technologies was similar with a beta-diversity between 19 and 25. Deviations within each setup were low with the alpha-diversity ranging from 2.23-2.93 (CAP) and 2.42-2.79 (UV). The water monitoring revealed similar results for pH value, conductivity, oxygen and temperature. No differences for the cortisol measurements and also the fish weight were determined. The results demonstrate CAP as a competitive and more energy efficient alternative to UV benefiting fish welfare and development in a similar way. The equal development of fish and water parameters and low energy consumption compared to UV makes CAP an energy efficient tool, likewise enhancing fish welfare.

papers.title: A cell-based screen identifies host-directed inhibitors and nutrient-conditional antimicrobials against intracellular S. flexneri dissemination
papers.abstract: Multidrug-resistant S. flexneri is a World Health Organization priority pathogen for which no universally licensed vaccine is currently available. Most antimicrobial screening platforms involve planktonic bacteria replicating in nutrient-rich medium, a condition that does not reflect the intracellular niche in which S. flexneri replicates and spreads and systematically excludes compounds whose activity depends on the host environment. Here, we screened the 1,581 compounds of the National Cancer Institute Diversity Set VII for inhibitors of S. flexneri dissemination in human colonic HT-29 monolayers by high-content microscopy. By applying sequential counter-screens, we identified six hits falling into two mechanistically distinct classes. Four compounds restricted dissemination without detectable antibacterial activity or host toxicity at the concentrations used. NSC310113 and Thiosangivamycin (NSC105827) implicate host matrix metalloprotease activity in cell-to-cell spread and host CDK2 in epithelial cell invasion. Two additional compounds, NSC45641 and NSC367428, were antibacte-rial only under nutrient-limited conditions and would have been described as inactive by conventional screening. NSC45641 is an adenine analog imposing a purine limitation reversible by adenine supplementation. The uracil analog NSC367428, whose activity requires the bacterial uracil phosphoribosyltransferase Upp, is consistent with perturbation of pyrimidine metabolism in both minimal medium and in HT-29 cells. Together, these findings demonstrate that cell-based dissemination screening of the NCI Diversity Set VII identified two classes of inhibitors that would likely be missed by conventional nutrient-rich medium screening, highlighting nutrient-conditional antimicrobials as promising starting points for developing treatments against intracellular pathogens.

papers.title: Evaluating WGS-based methods as an in silico replacement of phage typing for historical continuity and host association in Salmonella Typhimurium
papers.abstract: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (STm) poses a significant burden on public health worldwide. The Anderson phage typing scheme has historically supported surveillance, outbreak investigations and source attribution through associations between phage types and animal hosts. However, limitations inherent to the scheme have led to the gradual replacement of phage typing by whole-genome sequencing (WGS)-based methods. In this study, we applied statistical and machine learning approaches to 1,329 high-quality STm whole-genome sequences to compare phage typing with hierarchical clustering of core-genome multilocus sequence typing (HierCC) and the single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) address. We observed low congruence (< 0.60) between phage typing and WGS-based approaches. Nevertheless, a random forest model using WGS-based subtypes as features was able to predict all phage types with high specificity ([≥] 0.94) and at least 80% recall for 10 of the 24 analysed phage types. These included phage types of human and veterinary epidemiological importance, including DT193, DT104, DT2, DT40, DT56, DT9, and DT99. We then assessed whether WGS-based subtyping methods could replace the host-association feature of phage typing. At higher distance thresholds ([≥] 100) WGS-based subtyping methods were more informative of animal host species and displayed stronger host-associations than phage types for 11 of the 12 animal hosts, with significantly stronger associations for ducks, finches, and pigs (all p < 0.05). Thus, despite low congruence between phage types and WGS-based subtypes, our random forest model accurately predicted several epidemiologically important phage types, including those important to public health and veterinary surveillance, supporting its potential as an in silico alternative for those phage types. Finally, our findings suggest HierCC and SNP address methods can capture the host-association information historically derived from phage typing.

papers.title: From ancestral patterns of variation to the human condition: Leveraging disease phenotype associations and gene expression changes
papers.abstract: The shift in perspective to characterize the genetic basis of the human condition beyond fully fixed mutations opens many possibilities to scrutinize the nature of high-frequency derived variants in modern human genomes through the effect of the minor alleles, either already present in extant Pan relatives ("basal"), or found across most genomes of extinct hominins and likely introgressed into sapiens genomes. Here we present the results of intersecting a comprehensive catalog of such loci with the ClinVar and gnomAD databases, which provide associations with disease phenotypes, valuable to infer functional impacts. Recurrent disease associations highlight terms with sensorimotor processing and ataxia. Examining the impact of these variants in the GTEx database reveals striking differences between "basal" and "derived" patterns of variation: In contrast to minor alleles traceable to the Pan lineage ("basal variation"), minor alleles that are derived in extinct hominin genomes are found in highly constrained genomic regions in the GnomAD database, and are in general depleted of brain-specific effects in the GTEx database. Our Gtex analysis also highlights the cerebellum as the tissue with the most salient differences between major and minor (basal) alleles, pointing to the relevance of this brain region for understanding the evolution of our lineage. This finding is further reinforced by a Gene Ontology pathway analysis, which brings out metabolic terms, some specific to the cerebellum and glial cell types.

papers.title: The effects of selfing, limited seed dispersal and environmental persistence on the evolution of size-dependent sex allocation
papers.abstract: Sex allocation, the division of resources between male and female function, often varies as a function of size in cosexual plants. This variation is thought to evolve because fitness returns gained from allocating to each function are influenced by plant size, and many mechanisms have been proposed for why it should be so. Here, we explore how competing selfing and limited seed dispersal jointly shape the evolution of size-dependent sex allocation in an annual plant population where size is environmentally determined. First assuming that the quality of habitat patches changes every generation, we show that competing selfing favours increased femaleness with size, whereas limited seed dispersal selects in the opposite direction. Which of the two mechanisms prevails depends on the selfing and seed dispersal rates, as well as on the severity inbreeding depression. Then, we let patch-quality differences persist over several generations and show that such persistence generates an additional selective pressure on sex allocation when seed dispersal is limited. Environmental persistence favours larger plants to allocate more resource to female function, as producing more seeds increases the probability that their own offspring settle on their high-quality patch in the next generation.

papers.title: Genomic trinucleotide composition reflects context-dependent mutation spectra in plants and mammals
papers.abstract: Mutation rates vary substantially across mutation types and sequence contexts, yet it remains unclear how variation in the mutation spectrum shapes genome composition across species. Motivated by the strong cross-species relationship between CpG mutation rate and CpG content, we hypothesize that multi-nucleotide genome composition reflects the context-dependent mutation spectrum, with additional effects of GC-biased gene conversion (gBGC). To test this hypothesis, we develop a framework to determine the equilibrium trinucleotide composition from a context-dependent mutation spectrum, with and without incorporating the effects of gBGC. The trinucleotide frequencies predicted by our model based on polymorphism-derived mutation spectra of 25 plants and 10 mammals show good concordance with observed genomic trinucleotide compositions, and incorporating gBGC further improves agreement across all species, highlighting the pervasive influence of gBGC on genome composition. We further find that genome composition retains information about lineage-specific context-dependent mutation spectra, with strong correspondence within evolutionary clades but limited species-level specificity. In particular, trinucleotide abundance ratios correlate positively with the corresponding reciprocal mutation rate ratios, both across trinucleotide pairs within species and across species for the same trinucleotide pair. Together, our results demonstrate that genome composition encodes quantitative information about mutation processes and suggest that a single reference genome can inform mutational patterns in species lacking polymorphism data or direct measurements of mutation.

papers.title: Models show altered outcomes from evolution of standing genetic variation in response to a suppression gene drive
papers.abstract: Gene drives are commonly modelled as engineered inheritance-biasing systems with fixed performance, showing great potential for controlling disease vectors and other pests. Yet, natural populations contain standing genetic variation potentially capable of modifying drive transmission, resistance allele formation, and drive-associated fitness. This could lead to evolution in the population after the release of a drive system, potentially affecting the outcome. Here we use individual-based panmictic and spatial mosquito models to examine how standing genetic variation responds to the release of a homing drive configured for population suppression. Genetic variation affecting drive conversion efficiency showed a robust anti-drive response, evolving towards reduced conversion and resulting in inferior outcomes if rapid population elimination was avoided. In contrast, variation affecting embryo resistance and drive fitness cost showed context-dependent evolutionary responses associated with the spatial dynamics of the drive. These could evolve to either increase and inhibit the drive or decrease and improve drive outcomes. Evolving genetic variation in dispersal slightly increased successful elimination outcomes. Recessive deleterious variation acting through inbreeding depression reduced the minimum post-release population size, potentially increasing population elimination rates. However, its effects were not effective in the long-term since deleterious mutations were quickly purged among populations that persisted. Together, these results identify component and scenario-specific evolutionary trajectories based on drive pressure and available standing genetic variation. Thus, standing genetic variation may be treated as a dynamic part of theoretical gene drive modeling and could be worth experimentally quantifying for some possible release candidates.

papers.title: A naïve genome reveals the evolutionary dependence of CTCF functions
papers.abstract: The functions of genome regulatory proteins often emerge through long-term coevolution with their genomic and nuclear environments, complicating the distinction between intrinsic protein properties and context-dependent activities. The DNA-binding protein CTCF is a multifunctional regulator that plays central roles in genome organization and gene regulation across animals. Here, we investigated the behaviour of human CTCF in a deeply heterologous system by expressing it in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a lineage that diverged before the evolution of CTCF itself. Human CTCF was efficiently expressed, localized to the nucleus and associated with yeast chromatin, yet failed to establish robust sequence-specific binding or substantial transcriptional responses. Genome-wide analyses revealed no significant changes in chromatin accessibility, although modest footprinting and nucleosome-positioning effects were detected around predicted CTCF motifs. Together, our results suggest that chromatin association can occur independently of prior evolutionary history, whereas key aspects of CTCF target recognition and regulatory activity depend on long-term genome-protein coevolution.

papers.title: Power analysis for selection in allele-frequency time series.
papers.abstract: Allele frequencies tracked through time, from ancient DNA, museum collections or monitoring, offer a direct view of selection. Their value depends on whether the sampling design can distinguish change caused by selection from genetic drift and from the noise of sampling few individuals, often sequenced at low coverage. Researchers need to know how much power a design has before committing specimens and sequencing effort, which usually requires study-specific simulations. We present SPOT (Selection Power Over Time), a browser-based simulator that estimates the power to detect directional selection at a candidate locus from samples taken at several dates. Users describe the sampling design (dates, number of individuals, sequencing depth) and a biological scenario (inheritance system, generation time, effective population size, starting allele frequency, selection coefficient and dominance). Within seconds, SPOT simulates selection while accounting for sampling, genotype calling and drift, and sets the detection threshold from simulations without selection. Its sample-size planner shows how many individuals are needed to reach a target power. Conventional approaches, which model sampling error but not drift, overestimate power when drift is strong: in a museum insect case study, a threshold ignoring drift reported 69% power but called 10% of neutral loci selected instead of 5%; the drift-aware threshold gave 55%. SPOT agreed with the individual-based simulator SLiM in allele-frequency distributions, power and false-positive rates. Case studies of museum insects and human ancient DNA show how SPOT identifies detectable selection coefficients and helps allocate specimens and sequencing effort. SPOT is open source and runs without installation.

papers.title: Spatial and temporal drivers of genomic inbreeding in a declining population of yellow-bellied marmots
papers.abstract: Estimates of genetic diversity and effective population size are critical for predicting the resilience of natural populations to environmental change. We generated the first estimates of genetic diversity, effective population size and genomic inbreeding in a wild population of yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventer) studied continuously in western Colorado since 1962. Using 21 years of data from 284 individuals genotyped at 153,550 minimally filtered SNPs, including 17,393 neutral and unlinked SNPs, we found cryptic patterns of genetic subdivision and migration along a latitudinal gradient. A geographic cline in ancestry revealed a narrow (~900 m) genetic contact zone consistent with limited, unidirectional gene flow from south to north on the landscape. We also discovered a recent, severe decline in both census size and Ne following the winter of 2010 from which the population has yet to recover, contrasting prior trends of demographic expansion over the past century. Genomic inbreeding has remained elevated since this population decline, although long runs of homozygosity remain low in frequency despite pedigreed mating between relatives. Higher maternal inbreeding was associated with lower seasonal mass gain in offspring, consistent with intergenerational inbreeding depression in a trait predictive of annual survival. These findings indicate that while this well-monitored population has persisted at a low Ne with relatively high inbreeding, a recent, indeterminate census collapse and evidence for inbreeding depression in a key fitness-linked trait may threaten its future persistence.

papers.title: Hemodynamic and Yap1/Wwtr1-dependent epithelial-endothelial signaling establish fenestrated endothelial identity and permeability in the choroid plexus
papers.abstract: The choroid plexus (CP) produces cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and resides at the interface between CSF and circulating blood. How the CP establishes permeable endothelial identities and properties distinct from neighboring barrier-forming endothelium remains unknown. By developing new genetic and functional screening platforms in zebrafish, we identified blood flow-responsive KLF2 orthologues, klf2a and klf2b, as critical regulators of CP endothelial identity and permeability. Subsequent investigations linked these findings to hemodynamic and mechanosensitive Yap1/Wwtr1 signaling requirements. Expression analyses showed Yap1/Wwtr1 in endothelial and epithelial CP compartments, while epistatic analyses suggested that Yap1/Wwtr1 activity counteracts reduced hemodynamic inputs in the endothelium. Conversely, Yap1/Wwtr1 activity regulates epithelial expression of the VEGFA orthologue vegfab, which signals through endothelial Vegfr2 in CP vascular specialization. These findings define hemodynamic and Yap1/Wwtr1-dependent epithelial-endothelial signaling as crucial determinants of CP vascular specialization and propose that systemic and organ-specific fluid mechanics intersect to shape tissue environments generating unique cellular properties.

papers.title: Phosphorylation of the ER-plasma membrane tether E-Syt2 facilitates the loss of contact sites in mitosis
papers.abstract: Mitosis is associated with dramatic remodeling of intracellular organelles that supports their equal distribution between daughter cells. Recent investigations into membrane contact sites (MCS) show that they also remodel in mitosis with a significant loss of ER-plasma membrane CS (ERPMCS). However, the mechanisms governing this loss are unknown. Here we show that phosphorylation of the ERPMCS tether extended synaptotagmin 2 (E-Syt2) facilitates the loss of ERPMCS in mitosis. Preventing E-Syt2 phosphorylation in mitosis rescues the loss of ERPMCS. The persistence of ERPMCS is associated with delayed growth and progression through mitosis. This shows that E-Syt2 mitosis specific phosphorylation regulates its tethering potential and that the loss of ERPMCS is important for timely cell division.

papers.title: Targeted protein depletion in quiescent fission yeast cells using an auxin-degron system
papers.abstract: Quiescence is a reversible, non-proliferative cellular state in which cells can remain for extended periods of time while retaining the ability to re-enter the cell cycle upon exposure to favorable conditions. This physiological state is critical for a broad range of biological processes, from stress response in unicellular systems to differentiation and development in multicellular organisms. Surprisingly, despite its recognized roles in cell biology in diverse species, key aspects of the regulation of quiescence remain poorly understood. To investigate protein function specifically in quiescence, a conditional activation approach is critical, in particular for factors that are essential for cell viability. However, the efficacy of a number of such inactivation strategies in quiescent cells remained unknown. Using nitrogen-depleted fission yeast cells as a well-established model for quiescence, we probed two types of commonly-used approaches: a targeted method for the reversible inhibition of engineered kinases using non-hydrolyzable ATP analogs, and a more general system targeting protein depletion using an auxin-inducible degron. Here we show that the use of analog-sensitive kinases is unsuitable for quiescent fission yeast cells, as the ATP analog serves as a nitrogen source and induces cell cycle re-entry. We then demonstrate how coupling a degron tag with a specific auxin ligand allows for rapid, lasting and reversible protein depletion in quiescent cells, providing a powerful tool for investigating the regulation of this crucial and widespread cellular state.

papers.title: Identification of ATAD1 at Mitochondria-ER Contact Sites Reveals Its Role in Mitochondrial-to-ER Protein Transfer
papers.abstract: Mitochondria-ER contact sites (MERCs) play important roles in cellular functions such as lipid and Ca2+ transport and the regulation of mitochondrial dynamics. To better understand the functional diversity of MERCs, it is critical to identify proteins localized at these sites. Here, we employed CsFiND (Complementation assay using fusion of Split-GFP and TurboID) to identify MERC-associated proteins in HeLa cells. Proteomic and cell biological analyses identified ATAD1, a mitochondrial AAA-ATPase, as a MERC-associated protein. ATAD1 facilitates the transfer of GFP-Pex26{triangleup}C, a mislocalized peroxisomal membrane protein, from mitochondria to the ER. GFP-Pex26{triangleup}C is then degraded by the proteasome in a manner dependent on the ER-resident E3 ubiquitin ligase MARCH6. Notably, proteasome inhibition resulted in the accumulation of GFP-Pex26{triangleup}C at MERCs, suggesting that these sites may participate in this quality-control pathway. Together, these findings suggest a potential role for MERCs in the quality control of proteins mislocalized to mitochondria.

papers.title: Electrophysiological Comparison of Mechanosensitive PIEZO1 Channel Currents across Different Human Cell Types
papers.abstract: The detection of mechanical stress is essential for a wide range of physiological functions in humans, including touch sensation, hearing, and the maintenance of vascular myogenic tone. PIEZO1 is a mechanosensitive cation channel that is widely expressed in both neuronal and non-neuronal cells and plays critical physiological roles in multiple organs. However, the electrophysiological properties of endogenous PIEZO1-mediated mechanosensitive currents have not been systematically compared across different human cell types under identical experimental conditions. Here, the author compared the electrophysiological properties of endogenous human PIEZO1 (hPIEZO1) currents in four cultured human cell types: human aortic endothelial cells, human brain capillary endothelial cells, human fibroblast-like synoviocytes, and human osteoblast-like MG63 cells. Under whole-cell patch-clamp conditions, application of the PIEZO1 agonist Yoda1 robustly activated hPIEZO1-like currents in all four cell types. In excised outside-out patch recordings, application of positive pressure to membrane patches from these cells also elicited PIEZO1-like channel currents, which were markedly potentiated by Yoda1 and effectively inhibited by gadolinium, a non-selective cation channel blocker. Furthermore, the unitary current amplitudes of single channel events evoked by mechanical stimulation were comparable to those elicited by Yoda1 across all four cell types. Collectively, these findings provide electrophysiological evidence that endogenous PIEZO1 functions as a mechanosensor in diverse human cell types and suggest that PIEZO1 contributes to mechanically regulated physiological processes in multiple human organs.

papers.title: Protease shaving resolves the surface proteome of infection-derived extracellular vesicles and unmasks their inflammatory activity
papers.abstract: Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) produced and released by infected macrophages carry both host proteins and bacterial antigens, but whether these components face outward, are enclosed within vesicles, or are associated with co-isolated material remains unclear, limiting our understanding of their accessibility to recipient cells. We combined proteinase K shaving with quantitative proteomics to characterize the protease-accessible proteome of sEVs released by Salmonella-infected RAW264.7 macrophages. Host and bacterial proteins exhibited distinct responses to proteolysis. Of 1,368 proteins quantified, 246 were significantly decreased following digestion and a further 93 became undetectable. Among the depleted proteins, 26 carried independent topological evidence of surface exposure, spanning tetraspanins, integrins, MHC class I molecules, GPI-anchored proteins and membrane receptors, and the depleted fraction also included the immune mediators TNF-, CSF2RA, CD40 and MIF. Most detected Salmonella proteins resisted proteolysis and seven were significantly increased. Peptide-level analysis localized TNF- depletion to its extracellular domain, which fell by more than 3 log? relative to a cytoplasmic peptide measured in the same injection. Preservation of luminal sEV markers and two normalization-independent measures indicated that vesicle integrity was maintained. Despite removal of this protease-accessible fraction, vesicle bioactivity was not diminished: proteinase K-treated vesicles induced stronger Il6 expression and NF-{kappa}B/AP-1 signaling than untreated vesicles, with both responses sensitive to TNF- blockade and polymyxin B. Our findings together suggest that the protease-accessible protein fraction influences the immunostimulatory activity of infection-derived sEV preparations, with removal of the externally available coat of EVs being associated with enhanced inflammatory signaling.

papers.title: LUBAC ubiquitinates FADD and Caspase-8 through distinct catalytic mechanisms and limits TNF-induced apoptosis
papers.abstract: The linear ubiquitin chain assembly complex (LUBAC) is a critical regulator of tumor necrosis factor (TNF) signaling that promotes pro-survival responses and suppresses apoptosis. Linear ubiquitination of the TNFR1-associated complex II components FADD and Caspase-8 has been reported, but whether they are direct LUBAC substrates, how they are modified, and what the modification does remain poorly understood. Here, we show that loss of HOIP, which destabilizes the LUBAC complex, sensitizes HCT116 cells to TNF-induced apoptosis, and that TNF induces linear ubiquitin-reactive species on endogenous FADD and Caspase-8. Using purified proteins, we demonstrate that FADD and Caspase-8 are direct LUBAC substrates with different catalytic requirements. Efficient FADD ubiquitination requires HOIL-1L in addition to HOIP, consistent with a priming-and-extension mechanism, whereas Caspase-8 is ubiquitinated by HOIP-containing subcomplexes lacking HOIL-1L. A complex containing FADD, Caspase-8, and RIPK1 formed independently of LUBAC activity, but pharmacological inhibition of HOIP increased Caspase-8 processing within the FADD-associated pool, and Met1-ubiquitinated FADD showed reduced binding to Caspase-8 in vitro. Mapping identified four death domain lysines that each support LUBAC-dependent FADD ubiquitination. In FADD-deficient cells, a FADD-diubiquitin fusion attenuated TNF/cycloheximide-induced apoptosis relative to wild-type FADD, whereas a lysine-less FADD supported apoptosis with delayed kinetics. Together, these findings identify FADD and Caspase-8 as direct LUBAC substrates modified through distinct catalytic routes and support a model in which ubiquitination of FADD limits productive engagement with Caspase-8.

papers.title: Human eIF3 and eIF5 coordinate AUG recognition to sustain energy homeostasis
papers.abstract: Precise translation initiation is essential for efficient production of proteins; missing or mis-selecting the canonical start site can have detrimental consequences. Past research identified several initiation factors governing start codon selection accuracy in yeast, but the increasing complexity of higher eukaryotes have limited similar research in mammalian cells. We present an in cellulo study of knock-in mutants of the eIF3c subunit of the multitasking eIF3 complex that disrupt eIF3's interaction with eIF5, thereby preventing functional binding of eIF5 to pre-initiation complexes. This selectively relaxes start site selection stringency and reduces initiation sensitivity, leading to altered translation efficiency for nearly 600 proteins. Proteins with N-terminal targeting signals were among those especially affected, resulting in impaired mitochondrial function. These findings establish the first direct causal link between an initiation factor, stringent start site recognition, and impaired mitochondrial respiration and glycolytic activity, implicating the eIF3-eIF5 interaction as a key regulator of energy homeostasis.

papers.title: Poxvirus-induced concurrent activation of SAMD9 and ERK establishes a unique immune state with heightened IFN-I responses to danger signals
papers.abstract: Mammalian poxviruses must overcome the cellular restriction factor SAMD9 to establish productive infection. SAMD9 is a widely expressed cytoplasmic sensor of double-stranded nucleic acids (dsNA) that induces type-1 interferon (IFN-I) responses and possesses anticodon-nuclease activity targeting tRNAphe specifically. To counteract SAMD9, poxviruses have evolved dedicated antagonists, including myxoma virus (MYXV) M062, which blocks both dsNA sensing and tRNAphe-nuclease activity. However, the significance of tRNAphe depletion during poxvirus infection has remained unclear. Here, we showed that mammalian poxviruses exhibit an unexpected enrichment of phenylalanine within their proteomes and preferentially utilize UUU phenylalanine codon. In contrast, host interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) have lower phenylalanine frequencies than poxviruses and instead preferentially utilize UUC codon. Together with the known preferentially translational impairment of UUU-rich transcripts following SAMD9-mediated tRNAphe depletion, these findings suggest a mechanism by which unobstructed SAMD9 disproportionally restricts poxvirus protein synthesis while preserving host antiviral protein production. Next, using an M062-deficient MYXV mutant ({Delta}M062R), we characterized the cellular consequences of unrestricted SAMD9 activation. Unlike vaccinia virus lacking the SAMD9 antagonists C7 and K1 (VACV-{Delta}C7L/K1L), {Delta}M062R infection induced robust ERK1/2 signaling and preserved cell growth despite SAMD9 activation. Meanwhile, {Delta}M062R infection sustained expression of antiviral and proinflammatory proteins while restricting viral protein synthesis. This established a unique cellular state characterized by heightened responsiveness to subsequent innate immune stimulation. These findings identify a previously unrecognized interaction between SAMD9-mediated translation control and ERK1/2 signaling that renders a buffering effect to catastrophic SAMD9-mediated translation shutdown and thus provide new insight into antiviral restriction and innate immune regulation.

papers.title: Two CntT methyltransferases from Actinosynnema mirum and Pseudomonas aeruginosa reveal conserved opine-type metallophore methylation but divergent biological roles
papers.abstract: Opine-type metallophores have been discovered in mono- and diderm bacteria, where they allow zinc import under conditions of severe deficiency, a situation often found in natural environments. Whilst this family of metallophores is relatively well characterised, their modes of action in the organisms in which they are found remain poorly documented. In the present study, we identified and characterized two homologous SAM-dependent methyltransferases from the monoderm Actinosynnema mirum and the diderm Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteria. We showed that the corresponding AmCntT (Amir_3913) and PaCntT (PA1921) enzymes methylate their cognate opine-metallophores, staphylopine and pseudopaline, respectively. Crystal structure of AmCntT established key structural features that are unique to this family of methyltransferase, and residues putatively involved in substrate stabilization were probed by site directed mutagenesis. Further investigation showed that, unlike the staphylopine from A. mirum, which is recovered in its methylated form in the extracellular medium, pseudopaline methylation occurred only under certain stress conditions and was only detected for an intracellular pool of pseudopaline, hence suggesting a role in its degradation in P. aeruginosa. Altogether, our data revealed a new common component of the A. mirum and P. aeruginosa opine-metallophore pathways respectively involved in staphylopine and pseudopaline methylation that appears to have distinct functional implications in each organism.

papers.title: Legionella pneumophila DenR is a bacterial S-acyltransferase for the human GTPase NRAS
papers.abstract: In eukaryotic cells, the covalent attachment of palmitic acid to cysteine residues is catalyzed by the DHHC superfamily of membrane-embedded protein acyltransferases (DHHC-PAT). Here, we discovered that the bacterial pathogen Legionella pneumophila codes for its own protein acyltransferase, DenR, which hijacks host palmitoylation. Unlike the DHHC-PATs, DenR is a cytosolic protein that peripherally associates with membranes via binding of PI3P lipids through its carboxy-terminal domain. PI3P binding allosterically activates the palmitoyltransferase activity of its N-terminal circularly permuted NlpC/P60 papain-like domain, resulting in palmitoylation of the host GTPase NRAS at cysteine 181 and thereby anchoring NRAS to membranes of the Legionella-containing vacuole. Importantly, DenR-mediated S-acylation was insensitive to 2-bromopalmitate treatment, which inhibits cellular protein palmitoylation, suggesting that DenR represents a novel class of cytosolic S-acyltransferase.

papers.title: Cryo-EM-based examinations of honey bee colony losses reveal structural insights into acute bee paralysis virus maturation and mechanical carriage
papers.abstract: Honey bee colony losses pose a complex and significant agricultural problem in the United States and Europe, which has also been linked to viruses. As opposed to a purely sequence-based approach, we used cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) as an alternative sequencing- and culture-independent diagnostic tool to investigate viral pathogens associated with colony losses in the state of Texas. By purifying a limited number of viral particles directly from degraded hive remains, we could establish the identity of acute bee paralysis virus (ABPV) at the species level without prior sequencing data at 3.1 &Aring resolution, reconstructed of only 443 particles. We showed that small hive beetles carry mature ABPV virions, both within their digestive tract and attached to their cuticle. We successfully utilized cryo- EM to infer active ABPV replication from honey bee carcasses by reconstructing the virion structure of immature provirions at 2.35- and 2.53 [A], respectively, even several days after the collapse, despite the degradation of negative-strand RNA intermediates. Structural characterization of these immature particles revealed that ABPV capsids assemble around a condensed genomic core with the nucleic acid gradually expanding to occupy the capsid interior, ultimately bringing the VP0 structural protein in contact with VP3, which cleaves VP0 to structural proteins VP2 and 4. Together, our findings establish cryo-EM as a complementary diagnostic approach that simultaneously enables viral identification, replication-state assessment, and structural characterization, providing unprecedented insights into the maturation process of aparaviruses, a lineage of honey bee-infecting picorna-like viruses at the forefront of colony losses.

papers.title: A simplified protocol for the generation of apical-out human bladder organoids in suspension using a rotating bioreactor
papers.abstract: Bladder organoids are commonly generated in extracellular matrix domes, where apical surfaces line an enclosed central lumen, limiting experimental accessibility. Suspension-based systems have been explored to generate polarity-reversed organoids, but current models are often derived from cancer cells, remain incompletely characterized or rely on highly specialized scaffolds. Here, we describe a rapid and scalable approach to generate apical-out human bladder organoids (hBOs) from primary bladder epithelial cells using a rotating bioreactor system with minimal extracellular matrix scaffolding. Organoids form within 8 days and exhibit an apical-out phenotype with outward-facing umbrella-like cells. These apical-out hBOs tolerate 100% pooled human urine for up to 4 hours and can be infected with uropathogenic E. coli, recapitulating hallmarks of infection such as the formation of intracellular bacteria communities. Overall, the apical-out configuration enables direct access to the umbrella cell layer, thereby simplifying experimental manipulation, including infection and treatment assays under physiological conditions.

papers.title: Understanding the dynamics of Telomerase-RNP complex in the human malaria parasite
papers.abstract: Amongst the human malaria causing species, P. falciparum exhibits an interesting telomere-telomerase (TERT) dynamics. In a striking contrast to humans, which have 10-15 kb long telomeres, parasite telomeres are shorter (1-2 kb) and are maintained by a very large Pf TERT (2.5 times bigger than hTERT) and its structural RNA (Pf TR is 5 times bigger than hTR). Till date, there are no studies on Telomerase-RNP complex in the malaria parasite. The RNP complex comprises of diverged TERT and RNA-interacting proteins (Dyskerin, GAR1, NHP2, NOP10, TCAB1) and structural TR. Interestingly, Pf TR undergoes stage-dependent transcription with non-uniform (heterogeneous) transcript length. The levels of Pf TR transcripts are much higher than that of Pf TERT, suggesting that Pf TR may have scaffolding non-coding RNA roles beyond TERT function. We also observed differential expression of Pf TERT and TR-interacting RNPs with non-stoichiometric cellular abundance. These RNPs can form higher-order complexes, which can be independent of TERT and TR. Through super-resolution microscopy (STORM), we observed distinct perinuclear localization of Pf TERT in ring, trophozoite and schizonts. Genotoxic and oxidative stress conditions affected the expression and subcellular fractionation of plasmodial Telomerase-RNP complex proteins (especially GAR1, NOP10), hinting towards their probable TERT-independent roles. Immunoprecipitation of Telomerase-RNP complex revealed specific enrichment of NOP10 and HSP90, hinting towards variable binding affinities of RNP proteins to Pf TERT. Our results suggest dynamics in the Telomerase-RNP assembly may allow them to perform both canonical and non-canonical functions to support intracellular parasite survival in evolutionary distinct hosts.

papers.title: A 6-week all-liquid caloric restriction diet reduced abundance of some butyrate-producing bacteria while increasing abundance of mucin-degrading bacteria
papers.abstract: Caloric restriction diets are a common diet strategy to reduce excess weight and obesity. The diets work by lowering the number of calories or energy input below a human's normal energy expenditure creating an energy deficit. Caloric restriction diet meals can be composed of whole foods, meal replacement shakes, or a combination of the two. While the effects of these diets on human metabolism are well-known, the effects of these diets and the durability of these effects on the human gut microbiome are less well-known. The objective of this work was to investigate the effects of a 6-week all-liquid caloric restriction diet on the human gut microbiota using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing to assess changes in diversity, community composition, and predicted function. We found that during the diet period beta-diversity shifts significantly away from what it was before the intervention (baseline), and returns to baseline a week after the diet. During the diet period we also observed a decrease in abundance of fiber-degrading and butyrate-producing bacteria with a simultaneous increase in abundance of mucin-degrading bacteria with a return to baseline level abundances in the post-diet period. Despite a liquid diet relatively high in carbohydrate (59% carbohydrate, 25% fat, 16% protein), predicted function analysis showed a shift in substrate preference away from dietary carbohydrates towards protein and host-glycans during the diet period. These findings suggest that despite the overall high carbohydrate content all-liquid caloric restriction diets deprive the gut microbiota of their preferred nutrient source due to the overall decline in calorie delivery which forces them to consume alternative nutrient sources like protein and host-glycans.

papers.title: Rapid development of E. coli resistance to Bdellovibrio predation during short-term co-culture
papers.abstract: When E. coli ML35 is co-cultured with Bdellovibrio sp. NC01 over 72 hours, prey populations initially experience a 3-log reduction, but then partially recover to ~20% of starting density. Population recovery is correlated with emergence of irregular colonies, which are distinct from typical circular ML35 morphotype. ML35 populations do not recover when co-cultured with Bdellovibrio bacteriovorus HD100, and irregular colonies are not observed in HD100 co-cultures or in prey-only controls. Whole-genome sequencing of clonal lines of irregular and circular morphotypes from three independent replicate assays confirmed they are derived from ML35. ML35-irregular is resistant to killing by Bdellovibrio sp. NC01 but susceptible to killing by HD100, indicating strain-specific predation resistance. Analysis of sequencing data showed that all three ML35-irregular lines and all three ML35-circular lines carry a mutation in rfbG, annotated as dTDP-rhamnosyl transferase involved in O-antigen synthesis. Two ML35-irregular lines have distinct IS element insertions in rfbG; the third has a substitution introducing a premature stop codon near the C-terminus. Two ML35-circular lines have the same missense mutation in rfbG, whereas the third has a nonstop mutation. Overall, these data suggest that rfbG may be under selective pressure during NC01 co-culture and that O-antigen may play a role in predation resistance. Further work, such as phenotypic testing of ML35-circular lines and reverse genetics experiments, are needed to clarify how rfbG affects prey susceptibility to Bdellovibrio predation.

papers.title: Characterizing the Effects of Filtration on Microbial Diversity, Reproducibility, and Genome Recovery from Wastewater
papers.abstract: Filtration is widely used in wastewater microbiome workflows, but how pore size, filtration tactics, and sampled fraction shape microbial profiles across sequencing approaches remains unclear. We compared direct and sequential filtration of wastewater through 3-, 0.45-, and 0.22- micro meter filters and analyzed filter-retained and corresponding filtrates using 16S rRNA gene and ITS amplicon sequencing, shotgun metagenomics, and metatranscriptomics. Filtrates generally yielded higher microbial alpha diversity but greater between-replicate variability, whereas filters produced more reproducible bacterial DNA profiles. Fraction-dependent differences were strongest for fungal and DNA viral communities, which separated between filters and filtrates, while bacterial DNA communities were largely shared across fractions. These patterns demonstrate that pore size does not act as a strict size cutoff in wastewater for bacteria. DNA viruses were consistently enriched in filtrates, which also yielded more viral genomes. In contrast, filters yielded more bacterial metagenome-assembled genomes, but overall bacterial genome recovery was limited. Bacterial and viral metatranscriptomic profiles were comparatively variable and did not support selection of a single preferred fraction for RNA-based recovery. Direct and sequential filtration also produced distinct profiles at the same terminal pore size, indicating that filtration history influences the recovered community. Together, these results suggest that wastewater processing workflow should therefore be selected according to the intended use case.

papers.title: Real-world longitudinal multi-omics separates weight-loss-associated responses to incretin agonists from a broader response not dependent on weight loss
papers.abstract: The benefits of incretin agonists, including glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists, are largely attributed to glycemic control and weight loss, as these therapies enhance insulin secretion, suppress glucagon release and delay gastric emptying to produce satiety. Yet treatment is also associated with lower risk of cardiometabolic, renal and other chronic diseases. Whether these broader benefits depend on weight loss itself or reflect direct effects of treatment on physiology remains unclear, as does the basis of the marked variation in how patients respond. Resolving these questions has been difficult because weight loss and drug effects occur together, and because molecular studies of treated patients have been limited in scope. Here we profiled paired plasma samples collected before and after treatment from 165 individuals drawn from DynamiQ, a biorepository that links plasma samples to longitudinal clinical records, combining mass spectrometry-based proteomics, a targeted inflammation proteomics panel (NULISAseq) and non-targeted metabolomics to capture metabolic function, inflammation and markers of chronic disease. Treatment was associated with broad remodeling of the plasma proteome and metabolome, but the extent to which this remodeling depended on weight loss differed across the molecular layers. The metabolome carried a lipid signature that scaled with the weight lost, whereas proteomic and inflammation-panel changes largely did not depend on weight loss. Among these changes, treatment was associated with lower circulating mitochondrial oxidative proteins and cardiolipins, consistent with relief of lipid-driven metabolic stress, and with a shift of the inflammation panel toward a less inflamed state. A metabolic aging clock showed that age acceleration decreased by a mean of 2.96 years after treatment (95% confidence interval -4.95 to -0.98; P = 3.7 x 10-3), a change that did not depend on weight loss or on the interval between samples, with the largest reductions in participants starting from the highest age acceleration, most of whom had diabetes. Treatment-associated features overlapped with features associated with cardiometabolic, renal and hepatic disease. Before treatment, higher systemic inflammation, reflecting chronic tissue stress and repair, was associated with less subsequent weight loss. Together, these findings indicate that incretin agonist treatment is associated with lower markers of metabolic and inflammatory stress and with a younger metabolic age, changes that do not depend on weight loss, identify baseline inflammation as an axis of heterogeneity in treatment response, and suggest that biorepositories linking longitudinal multi-omic profiling to clinical records can relate drug pharmacodynamics to disease risk and to variation in patient response.

papers.title: TBACdb: a comprehensive database of tobacco bioactive compounds
papers.abstract: Tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum L.) contains diverse chemical constituents, but information on their biological activities, plant origins, supporting literature, and experimentally accessible standards remains fragmented. Here, we developed TBACdb (http://115.120.251.12:30003/), an integrated database of tobacco bioactive compounds. Starting from 5,139 tobacco-associated chemicals with CAS numbers, multi-source curation yielded 4,634 standardized compound records, including 2,377 compounds associated with reported biological activities and 166 compounds directly supported by tobacco-focused studies. TBACdb integrates 64,522 compound--bioactivity records, 12,465 compound--species associations, more than 3.7 million literature records, and 783 physical reference standards. The database provides chemical structures and physicochemical properties, biological activities, species origins, literature evidence, statistical analysis, external database links, and digital--physical compound mapping. TBACdb provides a centralized resource for tobacco compound exploration, candidate prioritization, and subsequent analytical and experimental investigation.

papers.title: Leaflet shape modulates canopy light-use efficiency by partitioning light more evenly among soybean leaves
papers.abstract: Modern soybean (Glycine max) canopies carry more leaves than they need, so yield gains depend on using light more efficiently. Lines carrying the narrow-leaflet allele of GmJAG1 yield as much as broad leaflet lines despite having less leaf area. We asked whether leaflet shape raises canopy light capture or light-use efficiency. To separate the two, we simulated 530 measured plots of broad- and narrow-leaflet near isogenic lines at two sites in the Helios three-dimensional ray-tracing model. We compared these simulations with a one-dimensional model of identical leaf physiology and with field data, then mapped the traits by genome-wide association. In the simulations, both leaflet types absorbed similar fractions of light, but narrow-leaflet canopies had 4-7% higher light-use efficiency. The one-dimensional model recovered little to none of this gain, tying it to canopy structure, where narrow leaflets partitioned light more evenly among leaves at each depth. In the field, narrow lines matched broad-line yield with 12% less leaf area, and yield per unit leaf area (+13.7%) mapped to GmJAG1, as did leaflet shape and simulated traits. With less leaf area, narrow-leaflets canopies are thus predicted to absorb as much light as broad-leaflet canopies and use it more efficiently. As a heritable single-gene trait, leaflet shape could complement leaf-biochemical routes to improved photosynthesis.
